subtype_info: Chronic Trichuris trichiura infection of the ileocecal valve mimicking malignancy
title: Chronic Trichuris trichiura Infection Presenting as Ileocecal Valve Swelling Mimicking Malignancy
case_text:
A 46-year-old man complained of two episodes of bright red rectal bleeding during the past month. He also had diarrhea intermittently for the past two months associated with visible mucus in the stool. There was no significant previous medical illness, and physical examination was also unremarkable. Proctoscopic examination showed two internal hemorrhoids which were banded. Due to the history of prolonged diarrhea, colonoscopy was arranged for him. This revealed a swollen ileocecal valve associated with superficial ulceration (Figure 1). Biopsies were taken to rule out possible malignancy. The current diagnosis was internal haemorrhoids with possibility of colonic malignancy. A simple stool for microscopic examination was not ordered for him since the clinical diagnosis pointed towards malignancy.
Histopathological examination of the biopsied tissue from the ileocecal valve showed moderate lymphocytic cell infiltrates in the mucosa together with cross sections of an adult female nematode (Figure 2). The cross section of the worm body wall displayed cuticle with prominent annulations, hypodermis with hypodermal nuclei, contractile portion of muscle, and sarcoplasmic portion of muscle with nuclei (Figure 3). Multiple ova were observed within the body, and these ova appeared to have terminal plugs (Figure 4). The cross section of the caudal end revealed two caudal papillae (Figures 5(a) and 5(b)). These findings were consistent with an adult female Trichuris trichiura. He was treated with oral albendazole 200 mg daily for three days and remained asymptomatic on followup several months later.

   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Soil-Transmitted Helminths
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Chronic Trichuris trichiura infection of the ileocecal valve mimicking malignancy
